problem.text: In rectangle $ABCD$, $\overline{AB} = 20$ and $\overline{BC} = 10$. Let $E$ be a point on $\overline{CD}$ such that $\angle CBE = 15^\circ$. What is $\overline{AE}$?

steps.title: Where to start: turn the $15^\circ$ into special angles
steps.body: Draw the rectangle with $A$ top left, $B$ top right, $C$ bottom right, $D$ bottom left, so $E$ is on the bottom side. The given angle $15^\circ$ is not a special-triangle angle, but it is the difference of two that are: $15^\circ = 75^\circ - 60^\circ$. That is the clue to cut a $60^\circ$ angle off the angle at $E$ and get a $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle.

your_turn.prompt: Triangle $BCE$ has a right angle at $C$. What is $\angle BEC$?

steps.title: Draw $EX$ to make an isosceles triangle
steps.body: Draw a segment from $E$ to a point $X$ on $BC$ so that $\angle CEX = 60^\circ$. Then $\angle XEB = 75^\circ - 60^\circ = 15^\circ$, which equals $\angle XBE$. So triangle $XEB$ is isosceles; call $XB = XE = a$. Triangle $XEC$ is a $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle with hypotenuse $XE = a$ and the $60^\circ$ angle at $E$.

your_turn.answer: $EC$ is opposite the $30^\circ$ angle at $X$, so $EC = \frac{a}{2}$; $CX$ is opposite $60^\circ$, so $CX = \frac{a\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

steps.title: Use $BC = 10$ to find $a$
steps.body:
The points $B$, $X$, $C$ lie in order on side $BC$, so
$$a + \frac{a\sqrt{3}}{2} = 10.$$

your_turn.prompt: Solve for $a$ and rationalize the denominator.

steps.title: Find where $E$ sits on $DC$
steps.body: Now that $a$ is known, the short leg $EC = \frac{a}{2}$ tells us where $E$ is along the bottom side, whose length is $DC = AB = 20$.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: So $DE = DC - EC = 20 - (20 - 10\sqrt{3}) = 10\sqrt{3}$. Triangle $ADE$ has a right angle at $D$, with legs $AD = 10$ and $DE = 10\sqrt{3}$. They are in the ratio $1 : \sqrt{3}$, so it is a $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle and the hypotenuse is twice the short leg: $AE = 2\cdot 10 = 20$. (Check: $10^2 + (10\sqrt{3})^2 = 400 = 20^2$.) The answer is **(E)**.

wrong_choices.B: $10\sqrt{3}$ is the length $DE$, not $AE$. It comes from stopping one step early: $AE$ is the hypotenuse of right triangle $ADE$, so it must be longer than $DE$.
